modernize-use-auto.title: Use 'auto' for variable declarations
modernize-use-auto.summary: Improves readability by using 'auto' instead of lengthy or complex type names.
modernize-use-auto.why: Long or complex type declarations clutter the code and make refactoring difficult. Using 'auto' forces the compiler to deduce the type, which eliminates visual noise and prevents accidental implicit conversions.
notes: Use 'auto' wherever explicitly specifying the type is unnecessary for readability.
Particularly useful for iterators, complex template types, and lambdas.

modernize-use-override.title: Use 'override' specifier
modernize-use-override.summary: Ensures that virtual functions actually override a base class function.
modernize-use-override.why: Without the 'override' specifier, a slight mismatch in the function signature (like a missing 'const') will silently create a new virtual function instead of overriding the intended one. The 'override' keyword turns this silent bug into a compile-time error.
notes: Always use 'override' for virtual functions overriding a base class.
Do not use 'virtual' and 'override' together; 'override' implies 'virtual'.

performance-unnecessary-value-param.title: Pass by const reference instead of value
performance-unnecessary-value-param.summary: Prevents unnecessary copies of expensive-to-copy objects when passed to functions.
performance-unnecessary-value-param.why: Passing objects like std::string or std::vector by value triggers a copy constructor. If the function only needs to read the object, passing by const reference (&) avoids this costly memory allocation and copying.
notes: Cheap-to-copy types (like int, float, bool) should still be passed by value.
If you intend to modify or store the parameter, passing by value and using std::move might be appropriate.

cppcoreguidelines-init-variables.title: Initialize all variables
cppcoreguidelines-init-variables.summary: Ensures that every variable is initialized at the time of declaration.
cppcoreguidelines-init-variables.why: Uninitialized variables lead to undefined behavior, which can cause unpredictable bugs, memory corruption, and security vulnerabilities. Always initialize variables to a safe default.
notes: Prefer brace initialization '{}' as it prevents narrowing conversions.

bugprone-use-after-move.title: Do not use an object after it has been moved
bugprone-use-after-move.summary: Prevents accessing an object whose resources have already been transferred via std::move.
bugprone-use-after-move.why: After an object is moved using std::move(), it is left in a valid but unspecified state. Accessing its value or calling methods on it leads to undefined behavior or crashes.
notes: Only use an object after moving it if you are assigning a completely new value to it.

modernize-use-nullptr.title: Use 'nullptr' instead of 'NULL' or '0'
modernize-use-nullptr.summary: Replaces legacy C-style null pointer constants with the type-safe 'nullptr'.
modernize-use-nullptr.why: The macros 'NULL' and '0' are just integers. This can lead to ambiguity in function overloading (where an integer overload might be called instead of a pointer overload). 'nullptr' has its own dedicated type (std::nullptr_t).

performance-for-range-copy.title: Avoid unnecessary copies in range-based for loops
performance-for-range-copy.summary: Prevents accidental object copies when iterating over a container.
performance-for-range-copy.why: Using 'for (auto item : container)' copies every element in the container. If the elements are expensive to copy (like strings or complex structs), this significantly degrades performance.
notes: Use 'auto&' if you need to modify the elements in the container.

bugprone-macro-parentheses.title: Wrap macro parameters in parentheses
bugprone-macro-parentheses.summary: Ensures that macros evaluate expressions correctly by enforcing operator precedence.
bugprone-macro-parentheses.why: Because macros are simple text replacements, passing an expression (like 'a + b') into a macro can break operator precedence, leading to catastrophic logical errors.
bugprone-macro-parentheses.exampleBefore:
#define MULTIPLY(x, y) x * y
int result = MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3); // Evaluates to 1 + 2 * 3 = 7
bugprone-macro-parentheses.exampleAfter:
#define MULTIPLY(x, y) ((x) * (y))
int result = MULTIPLY(1 + 2, 3); // Evaluates to ((1 + 2) * (3)) = 9
notes: Whenever possible, avoid macros entirely and prefer 'constexpr' functions or inline templates.

cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-vararg.title: Do not use variable arguments (varargs)
cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-vararg.summary: Avoid C-style variable length argument lists.
cppcoreguidelines-pro-type-vararg.why: Varargs bypass the C++ type system entirely. Passing the wrong type to a vararg function will not cause a compiler error, but will crash the program at runtime. Modern C++ provides safer alternatives.

readability-identifier-naming.title: Follow standard identifier naming conventions
readability-identifier-naming.summary: Enforces consistent naming for variables, functions, and classes.
readability-identifier-naming.why: Inconsistent naming makes the codebase hard to read and maintain. Sticking to a unified convention (e.g., camelCase for variables, PascalCase for classes) improves collaboration.
notes: Ensure your clang-tidy configuration specifies the exact naming conventions your team uses.
